title: Abdominal epilepsy, an uncommon cause of chronic and recurrent abdominal pain: a case report
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of paroxysmal, recurrent abdominal pain localized to the epigastric region. The pain was burning in nature, of gradual onset, nonradiating, lasted about 30 minutes per episode, and occurred without specific periodicity. There was no relation to food intake and no clear aggravating or alleviating factors. He reported associated bloating but denied nausea, vomiting, alteration of consciousness, or confusion. He had a family history of epilepsy in his paternal grandfather but no family history of migraine. 

Over the preceding 2 years, he had been treated repeatedly for presumed peptic ulcer disease with proton pump inhibitors (rabeprazole, pantoprazole) and Helicobacter pylori triple therapy, as well as various analgesics, antihistamines, and multivitamins, all without relief. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver function tests, serum amylase, stool and urine examinations, and Helicobacter pylori serology, were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography, barium studies, and gastro-duodenoscopy showed no abnormalities.

At this point, abdominal epilepsy, abdominal migraine, and functional dyspepsia were considered.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Abdominal epilepsy was considered because the patient’s unexplained paroxysmal abdominal complaints and CNS symptoms fit the syndrome — “He had unexplained, paroxysmal gastrointestinal complaints, lethargy (CNS disturbance), suggestive EEG findings, and sustained response to anticonvulsant.”  
2. Abdominal migraine was considered given overlapping gastrointestinal and migraine-like features, but symptom duration in migraine is typically longer and EEG is normal in migraine — “The most common differential for AE is an abdominal migraine… Duration of the symptoms may be used to differentiate the two; the duration is longer in a migraine than in AE.”  
3. Functional dyspepsia was considered due to chronic epigastric pain with normal investigations and exclusion of organic disease, although it lacks EEG abnormalities and has nonspecific response patterns — “…initiation of antiepileptic can be crucial regardless of the EEG findings which could differentiate AE from an abdominal migraine or functional dyspepsia both of which may respond well to antiseizure medications.”
